reading.body:
Turnitin's AI detection tool addresses a real constraint in education: distinguishing student work from AI-generated text, but the company's data reveals significant blind spots around accuracy and privacy that limit its reliability as an integrity measure.

The company positions AI Detection as a solution to academic integrity by identifying when students use generative AI to write assignments. The tool integrates into learning management systems and covers diverse document types from essays to dissertations. This approach assumes detection accuracy is feasible and sufficient to solve the underlying problem of verifying authorship at scale across education institutions.

The data flags two critical gaps. False positive risk means the tool will flag human writing as AI-generated, creating harm without evidence of actual wrongdoing. Student data privacy under FERPA means institutions using this tool must handle sensitive educational records, but the data does not cover what happens to that data, how long it is retained, or who can access it. These are not edge cases but core operational risks for any detection system applied to minors and protected educational records.

The data does not indicate whether Turnitin's detection improves over time, how institutions should handle false positives, or whether the tool addresses the upstream question of why students resort to AI writing in the first place. It measures a symptom rather than the constraint it claims to solve.

profile_text.body:
Turnitin describes itself as an education technology company whose solutions promote academic integrity, streamline grading and feedback, deter plagiarism, and improve student outcomes. The company says its tools help guide responsible AI use, identify AI-generated writing, and assess securely, and it offers originality checking that compares student work against what it calls the world's largest academic database, including checks for AI writing inside a learning management system. It also describes device lockdown for exams, student ID verification, and secure digital exams that can run offline, plus similarity and AI writing scanning for documents, grant proposals, theses, and dissertations. Turnitin states that it uses AI selectively to assist in creating marketing materials, with AI-generated content reviewed, edited, and fact-checked by humans.

The company was founded in 1997 and is headquartered in Oakland. Two products are tracked for it under an education and research AI category. Turnitin AI Detection is described as AI writing detection for academic integrity, with noted false positive risk and student data privacy considerations under FERPA. Gradescope is listed with AI answer grouping, used by teachers for grading paper and digital assessments; its notes state it was found in research and not independently verified, that student age and privacy are not verified, and that pricing is a free basic plan for individual instructors with institutional plans by quote, with third parties reporting about $1 to $2 per student.

No litigation, MCP servers, SEC filings, or patent facts are recorded for Turnitin.
